topics.title: The Built-in node:test Runner
topics.summary: Write and run tests with no dependencies using node:test and node:assert, including hooks, async tests and watch mode.
topics.description:
Node includes a stable test runner. No Jest or Mocha needed for many projects.

### Basics
Import from `node:test`: `test`, `describe`, `it`, `before`, `after`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`, `mock`. Use `node:assert/strict` for checks.

### Running
* `node --test` finds files named `*.test.js`, `*.spec.js` or anything inside a `test/` folder and runs each in its own process
* `node --test path/to/file.test.js` runs one file
* `node --test --watch` re-runs on change
* `--test-name-pattern="user"` filters by name; `.only` plus `--test-only`, `.skip`, `.todo` mark tests
* `--test-reporter=spec | tap | junit | lcov`
* `--experimental-test-coverage` prints coverage

### Test structure
`describe` groups, `it`/`test` defines a case. Tests can be `async`. Subtests with `t.test()` are supported. Failing assertions throw, the runner marks the test failed and shows a diff.

### Good tests
1. **Arrange, act, assert**: set up data, call the code, check the result
2. One behaviour per test with a descriptive name
3. Independent: no test depends on another's side effects
4. Deterministic: control time, randomness, network
5. Fast: unit tests run in milliseconds

### Test pyramid
Many **unit tests** (functions, services), some **integration tests** (API with a test database), few **end-to-end tests** (full browser flows).

### Where to put them
Next to the code (`user.service.test.js`) or in `test/`. Keep fixtures in a `test/fixtures` folder.
keyPoints: node --test runs *.test.js files with no extra packages
describe/it/test, hooks and node:assert/strict are the basics
Tests should be independent, deterministic and fast
Use --watch during development and --experimental-test-coverage for coverage
Prefer many unit tests, fewer integration and e2e tests
pitfalls: Tests that depend on execution order or shared mutable state
Real network or real time inside unit tests

interview.q: Do you need Jest to test a Node app?
interview.a: No. node:test with node:assert is built in and covers describe/it, hooks, mocking, timers and coverage. Jest or Vitest add richer matchers, snapshots and watch UI which many teams prefer.

interview.q: What makes a good unit test?
interview.a: It tests one behaviour, is independent of other tests, deterministic (no real time, network or randomness), fast, and fails with a clear message.

topics.title: Jest and Vitest
topics.summary: Popular full-featured test frameworks: expect matchers, mocks, snapshots, watch mode, and when to choose which.
topics.description:
**Jest** and **Vitest** provide a batteries-included testing experience: runner, assertions (`expect`), mocking, snapshots, coverage and a watch mode.

### Comparison
| | Jest | Vitest |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Meta, huge ecosystem | Vite team, Jest-compatible API |
| Speed | Good | Faster start-up, native ESM and TypeScript |
| ESM support | Needs configuration | Works out of the box |
| Config | `jest.config.js` | `vitest.config.js` (or the Vite config) |
| Mock functions | `jest.fn()`, `jest.mock()` | `vi.fn()`, `vi.mock()` |
| Fake timers | `jest.useFakeTimers()` | `vi.useFakeTimers()` |

For new projects with ESM or TypeScript, **Vitest** is usually the smoother choice. Many existing codebases use Jest.

### Core API
* `describe`, `it`/`test`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`, `beforeAll`, `afterAll`
* `expect(value).toBe(x)` (strict equality), `toEqual` (deep), `toStrictEqual`, `toBeTruthy`, `toContain`, `toMatchObject`, `toThrow`, `rejects.toThrow`, `resolves`
* `toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)`, `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(n)`
* `toMatchSnapshot()` / `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` store expected output (use sparingly for logic)
* `it.each([[1,1,2],[2,3,5]])('add(%i,%i)=%i', ...)` for table-driven tests

### Running
`npx vitest` (watch), `npx vitest run` (once, for CI), `npx jest --watch`. Add `"test": "vitest run"` to scripts.

### Tips
* Reset mocks between tests (`vi.restoreAllMocks()`)
* Use `--coverage` with the v8 provider
* Test names should read like sentences
keyPoints: Jest and Vitest share a similar expect/describe/it API
Vitest has native ESM/TypeScript support and is fast; Jest is the long-time standard
toBe is strict equality, toEqual compares deeply
it.each runs table-driven tests
Snapshots are for stable output, not a replacement for assertions
pitfalls: Overusing snapshots so changes are blindly updated

interview.a: toBe uses Object.is (strict identity for objects), toEqual compares values recursively, so two different objects with the same contents are equal under toEqual but not under toBe.

interview.q: Why might a team choose Vitest over Jest?
interview.a: Faster execution, native ESM and TypeScript support without Babel configuration, and reuse of the Vite config, with a mostly Jest-compatible API.

topics.title: Testing APIs with supertest
topics.summary: Test Express/HTTP apps in-process without opening ports, using a test database and clean fixtures.
topics.description:
**supertest** calls your Express (or any `http.Server`) app directly and offers a fluent API to assert status, headers and body. It starts the app on an ephemeral port automatically, so there are no port clashes.

### Preparing the app
Export the app from `app.js` and keep `app.listen` in `server.js`. Then in tests: `import app from '../src/app.js'`.

### Writing tests
`await request(app).post('/users').send({ name: 'Ann' }).expect(201)` then check `res.body`. Chain `.set('Authorization', 'Bearer ...')`, `.query({ page: 2 })`, `.attach('file', path)`.

### Database strategy
| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| Real test database | Most realistic; use a separate DB (docker compose, Testcontainers) |
| In-memory (`mongodb-memory-server`, SQLite `:memory:`) | Fast, isolated |
| Mocks/fakes of repositories | Fast unit tests of services |

Reset data between tests: truncate tables or drop collections in `beforeEach`. Never point tests at production or shared development data.

### What to cover
* Happy paths and validation errors (400/422)
* Authentication (401) and authorisation (403)
* Not found (404) and conflicts (409)
* Pagination, sorting and filtering
* Error handler output shape

### Auth in tests
Create a user in a helper and sign a token with the test secret, or log in through the API once in `before`.

### Without supertest
Node 18+ lets you start the server on port 0 and use `fetch`: `const server = app.listen(0); const { port } = server.address();`. Close it in `after`.

### Contract and e2e
For browser flows use Playwright; for API contracts consider OpenAPI-based tools or Pact.
keyPoints: supertest sends requests to your app in-process and asserts the response
Export app separately from listen
Use a separate test database and reset it per test
Test error paths and auth, not just the happy path
Alternative: start on port 0 and call with fetch
pitfalls: Tests that run against a shared or production database
Leaving servers or DB connections open so the test process hangs

examples.explanation: supertest never binds a fixed port, so tests can run in parallel.

examples.explanation: Port 0 asks the OS for any free port.

interview.q: Why separate app and server files?
interview.a: So tests can import the app and let supertest handle the port, without the real server starting, and to avoid port conflicts and hanging processes.

interview.q: How do you keep API tests isolated?
interview.a: Use a dedicated test database, reset or truncate data before each test, create the fixtures each test needs and avoid depending on test order.

topics.title: Mocking, Stubs and Fake Timers
topics.summary: Replace slow or unpredictable dependencies with fakes: mock functions, module mocks, spies, time and HTTP.
topics.description:
A **mock** replaces a real dependency (database, email service, HTTP API, clock) with a controllable fake so the unit under test runs in isolation, quickly and deterministically.

### Vocabulary
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Stub** | Returns canned values |
| **Spy** | Wraps a real function and records calls |
| **Mock** | A fake that also verifies expected calls |
| **Fake** | A simple working replacement (in-memory repository) |

### In node:test
* `mock.fn(impl)` creates a function; inspect `fn.mock.calls`, `callCount()`
* `mock.method(obj, 'name', impl)` replaces a method (restore with `mock.restoreAll()` or the test context `t.mock`)
* `t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'Date'] })` then `tick(ms)` for **fake timers**
* `mock.module(...)` (experimental, run with `--experimental-test-module-mocks`)

### In Vitest / Jest
`vi.fn()`, `vi.spyOn(obj, 'method')`, `vi.mock('./email.js')`, `vi.useFakeTimers()`, `vi.setSystemTime(date)`.

### Mocking HTTP
Use `msw` or undici's `MockAgent` to intercept `fetch` calls and return responses, so you never hit real APIs in tests.

### Dependency injection beats module mocking
Pass dependencies as parameters (`createService({ repo, mailer })`). Tests then pass simple fakes without patching modules.

### Rules
1. Mock at the **boundary** (network, disk, time), not your own pure logic
2. Do not over-mock: tests that check mock calls only can pass while the real behaviour is broken
3. Restore mocks after each test
4. Keep at least some integration tests with the real database
keyPoints: Stubs return values, spies record calls, fakes are working substitutes
Use fake timers to test retries, debounce and expiry without waiting
Mock external boundaries such as HTTP, email and time
Dependency injection makes mocking easy
Restore mocks between tests
pitfalls: Mocking everything so tests no longer prove anything
Calling real external APIs from tests

examples.title: Fake timers and a spy
examples.explanation: Fake timers let a 200 ms delay finish instantly.

interview.a: A stub returns predefined data, a spy wraps a function and records how it was called, and a mock is a fake with expectations about calls. In practice libraries use "mock" for all of them.

interview.q: Why prefer dependency injection to module mocking?
interview.a: Passing dependencies as arguments needs no patching of the module system, is explicit and works the same in CommonJS and ESM, which keeps tests simple and less fragile.

topics.title: Code Coverage and CI
topics.summary: Measure which code your tests execute, interpret the metrics sensibly and run tests automatically in CI.
topics.description:
**Coverage** reports which lines, branches and functions ran during tests.

### Metrics
* **Line / statement**: how many lines executed
* **Branch**: both sides of every `if`/ternary/`??`
* **Function**: functions called at least once

### Tools
| Tool | Command |
|---|---|
| Node built in | `node --test --experimental-test-coverage` |
| c8 (V8 coverage) | `npx c8 node --test` |
| Vitest | `vitest run --coverage` (provider v8 or istanbul) |
| Jest | `jest --coverage` |

Reports: terminal table, `lcov` (for Codecov/Coveralls), HTML (`coverage/index.html`). Add `coverage/` to `.gitignore`.

### Thresholds
Fail the build when coverage drops, e.g. Vitest: `coverage: { thresholds: { lines: 80, branches: 70 } }`; Node: `--test-coverage-lines=80`.

### Interpreting
Coverage shows what was **not** tested; it does not prove tests are good. A test without assertions gives 100% coverage and zero value. Aim for meaningful coverage on business logic (70-90% is typical); do not chase 100% by testing getters or config.

### CI pipeline (GitHub Actions)
1. Checkout, set up Node with caching (`actions/setup-node` with `cache: npm`)
2. `npm ci`
3. `npm run lint`
4. `npm test -- --coverage`
5. Optionally build and upload coverage

Run on every pull request and make it a required check. Test against the Node versions you support with a **matrix**.

### Flaky tests
Fix or quarantine them quickly: they train people to ignore failures. Common causes are time, randomness, network and shared state.
keyPoints: Coverage measures executed code, not test quality
Use c8, Vitest or node --test coverage flags
Set sensible thresholds rather than 100%
Run lint and tests in CI on every pull request with npm ci
Eliminate flaky tests
pitfalls: Treating high coverage as proof of correctness
Letting flaky tests stay in the suite

examples.title: GitHub Actions workflow
examples.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test -- --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines=80
examples.explanation: The matrix runs the same job on three Node versions.

examples.title: Coverage output
examples.explanation: The last column lists line numbers that no test executed.

interview.a: No. It only means every line ran at least once. Missing assertions, untested edge cases and integration issues can still hide bugs.

interview.q: What is the difference between line and branch coverage?
interview.a: Line coverage counts executed lines; branch coverage checks that each decision path (both the if and else side, each logical operand) was taken, which is stricter and reveals untested conditions.
